summary: This work introduces Q-NEXUS, a heterogeneous quantum computing architecture with specialized modules for computation (small fixed-size QPUs), memory (STQM and RAQM), and communication (quantum bus), orchestrated by the Q-CHESS compiler. For RSA-2048 factorization, Q-NEXUS reduces physical qubit requirements from 0.9 M in a monolithic baseline to 0.19 M (with qLDPC codes) or 0.25 M, achieving 138× reduction in total qubits and 11× reduction in local couplers while maintaining comparable runtimes.
motivation: Quantum systems face a 'tyranny of numbers' scaling problem similar to early classical computing: expanding monolithic designs requires prohibitive growth in control wiring, readout channels, and cryogenic interconnects. Existing top-down QEC-driven analyses and bottom-up hardware constraints remain disconnected, missing opportunities to match hardware specialization to functional requirements.
method: The authors develop a modular architecture segregating fast (1 μs) 3-qubit superconducting QPUs from slow (50–1000 μs) long-coherence quantum memory (STQM using rare-earth ions or RAQM with active error correction), connected via teleportation-based quantum buses. Q-CHESS performs error-aware compilation with explicit accounting of timing mismatches, idling penalties, state-transfer costs, and scheduling across modules operating at different clock rates.
result: For 1,000 logical-qubit AQFT, heterogeneous architectures achieve 59× reduction in algorithmic error and 138× reduction in physical qubits (0.4 vs 49 M) using RAQM. For RSA-2048, B6 configuration with hierarchical memory, qLDPC codes in RAQM, and Adder accelerator requires 0.25 M qubits and 4.9 days; qLDPC-only variant (B3) needs 0.19 M qubits and 9.2 days, compared to 0.9 M qubits and 5 days in Gidney's monolithic baseline.
